name: Printing Consecutive Numbers Within a Specified Range (Case 2)
description: Construct a program that prints a sequence of numbers from 8 (inclusive) to 14 (inclusive).
code:
#Step 1: Iterate through the numbers in the sequence
for num in range(8, 15): 
    #Step 1.1: Print each number in the sequence
    print(num)

1.content: #Step 1: Iterate through the numbers in the sequence

commentList: Purpose: This line starts a loop so you can visit each number in the sequence; on each pass the variable num is set to the next value and the indented print statement runs for that value.

Syntax and semantics: range(8, 15) generates numbers starting at 8 and stopping before 15, so you get 8 through 14; for num in ... assigns each generated value to num in turn, and the trailing colon begins the loop body.

Common errors and misconceptions: Remember that range's stop value is exclusive—if you wrote range(8, 14) you'd stop at 13. Also be careful to include the colon and use correct indentation for the loop body, otherwise Python raises a SyntaxError or IndentationError.

Best practices: Use a clear loop variable name like num for readability, avoid changing num inside the loop, and if you need an inclusive end value think in terms of range(start, end + 1). If you want a different step, you can add a third argument like range(8, 15, 1).
Quick check you can do: if you're unsure what values range produces, call list(range(8, 15)) to see [8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14] before using the loop.

commentList: You use print(num) to output the current value of num so the program displays each number in the sequence (8 through 14).

You are calling the print function with num as its argument: print(...) tells Python to convert num to text and write it to the console. By default print adds a newline, so each number appears on its own line.

Be careful with indentation: if you don't indent print under the for loop, you will print only once after the loop finishes instead of printing every number. Also avoid typos in the variable name (e.g., printing numm) and remember that in Python 3 you must use parentheses around the argument.

As a best practice, keep print inside the loop to show each item, or if you want all numbers on one line use print(num, end=' ') or join a list into a single string and print once. Avoid modifying the loop variable inside print and remove debug prints in production code.

distractors.description: 1) Why you might pick this: you may believe that giving 14 as the stop value will include 14 in the output, so you set the stop to the end value you want. 2) What actually happens: the loop will produce numbers starting at 8 and stop before the stop value, so it will print up to 13 and omit 14. 3) Impact on the program: the sequence will be missing the final required number, so the output will be incomplete. 4) How this is wrong: the mistake is using a stop value that causes the loop to end too early; you are misimplementing the end bound. This line is therefore a plausible choice but incorrect because it fails to include the last desired number.

1) Why you might pick this: you may try to be cautious and give a larger stop value so you don't miss the final number, thinking any extra value won't hurt. 2) What actually happens: the loop will include all integers from 8 up to 15, so it prints one extra number beyond the required range. 3) Impact on the program: the output will include an extra value that should not be printed, producing an incorrect sequence. 4) How this is wrong: the stop value here overshoots the intended end, so you misimplement the end bound and produce too many numbers.

1) Why you might pick this: you might think a decimal like 14.0 is equivalent to 14 and will behave the same, so you write it out that way. 2) What actually happens: the language's range function requires integer arguments; passing a float will cause a runtime TypeError and the program will crash before printing anything. 3) Impact on the program: instead of producing the sequence, the program raises an error and stops. 4) How this is wrong: the mistake is using the wrong data type for the stop value; this misimplementation prevents the loop from running at all rather than producing the intended sequence.

You might choose 'for num in range(8, 13):' thinking the second argument is inclusive or suffering from an off-by-one boundary misconception. In Python, range(start, stop) generates values up to but not including stop. Therefore, range(8, 13) stops at 12, omitting the final values 13 and 14 required by the specification. The loop terminates prematurely.
